prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The author invites the reader to acknowledge that human nature is inherently equivocal, often leaving people uncertain of their direction upon waking each day.

- A church marquee's stark question about eternity ("smoking or non-smoking") reflects how mundane binary choices become stand-ins for larger existential decisions.

- The mention of a radio ministry's "wrong-answer button" suggests an anxious, almost fatalistic waiting for judgment or error in one's life choices.

- The extensive list of things to "count"—from grey hairs to broken bones to T cells—illustrates an obsessive, almost ritualistic method of measuring one's mortality and bodily existence.

- Through juxtaposing ordinary people's unconscious daily routines with weighty spiritual questions, the text suggests that profound existential contemplation is embedded within mundane, everyday life.

Keywords: Dear, Conflicted, Reader

outputs.L1:
My Dear Conflicted Reader,

Grant me this: that most of us possess an equivocal nature, and that upon waking, we have not yet settled which direction we're bound to take. Thus, you might observe a man driving to work in a shirt free of perfume and dye, or a woman with an excessive tan holding an orange flag in one hand and a Virginia Slim in the other—as though these were simply their appointed fates. Grant me, too, that both were likely contemplating some entirely different arrangement of things.

WHERE DO YOU WANT TO SPEND ETERNITY, the church marquee demands on the way to my son's school, SMOKING OR NON-SMOKING. I confess I had not considered the question of where, or in which direction, quite in those terms. The radio ministry insists that God has installed a wrong-answer buzzer, and we are all awaiting the moment it sounds...

Count your grey hairs
Count your chigger bites
Count your pills
Count the times the phone rings
Count your T-cells
Count your mosquito bites
Count the days since your last menses
Count the chickens you've eaten
Count your cankers
Count the storm candles
Count your stitches
Count your broken bones
Count the flies you killed before noon
outputs.L2:
Dear Reader in Turmoil,

Consider with me that most people carry within them a kind of doubleness, and that upon opening our eyes each morning, we haven't yet settled on which path we'll follow that day. Picture, then, a man commuting to his job wearing a shirt free of scent and dye, or a woman with a leathery, overworked tan gripping an orange flag in one hand and a Virginia Slim cigarette in the other—almost as though these roles were written into their fate from birth. Yet allow me to suggest that each of them was probably turning over entirely separate thoughts in their minds at that very moment.

On the route to my son's school stands a church sign posing the question: WHERE DO YOU WANT TO SPEND ETERNITY—SMOKING OR NON-SMOKING. I'll confess that framing the matter of destination, or direction, in quite this way had never crossed my mind before.

Meanwhile, some radio preacher insists that god keeps a buzzer ready for incorrect responses, and that all of humanity sits in suspense, waiting for it to sound...

Tally your silver strands
Tally your bug bites from chiggers
Tally your medications
Tally each ring of the telephone
Tally your T-cell count
Tally your mosquito welts
Tally the days elapsed since your period
Tally the poultry you've consumed
Tally your mouth sores
Tally your emergency candles
Tally your sutures
Tally your fractured bones
Tally the flies you've swatted dead before the stroke of noon
outputs.L3:
# On the Equivocal Nature of Waking Life

Let us begin by acknowledging something uncomfortable: human nature is fundamentally equivocal. We are creatures of contradiction, and this contradiction reveals itself most starkly in the simple, universal act of waking. Each morning, countless people rise from sleep without any clear sense of direction—not merely in the practical sense of what tasks await them, but in some deeper, more unsettling way. They blink into consciousness uncertain of who they are meant to be that day, what they believe, or which version of themselves will emerge to face the hours ahead. This is not dramatic existential crisis so much as quiet, persistent ambiguity—the low hum of not-knowing that underlies even our most routine mornings.

This uncertainty finds curious expression in the small, almost comic artifacts of everyday life. Consider the church marquee that poses eternity as a binary choice: "smoking or non-smoking." The crude humor of the phrase cannot fully mask its unsettling logic—that ultimate questions of salvation and damnation have been reduced to the same register as a restaurant seating preference. Yet perhaps this reduction is not merely absurd but revealing. We are creatures who need our infinite questions translated into finite terms, our cosmic stakes rendered as simple multiple-choice decisions, if only so that we might begin to comprehend them at all. The mundane becomes the vessel through which we smuggle in the profound.

A similar dynamic appears in the image of a radio ministry's "wrong-answer button"—a device, real or imagined, that seems to embody a particular kind of spiritual anxiety. There is something deeply fatalistic in this notion: the sense that one is always poised on the edge of error, that a buzzer might sound at any moment to announce one's failure before some unseen judge. This is waiting not for revelation but for correction, for the moment when the universe—or God, or conscience—signals that we have chosen incorrectly. It suggests a theology of dread, where faith is experienced less as comfort than as constant, low-grade apprehension.

This anxious vigilance extends into the body itself, manifesting in an extensive, almost obsessive practice of counting. We count our grey hairs as though tallying the encroachment of time. We count broken bones as evidence of accumulated damage, small fractures that map our vulnerability. We count T cells, that most modern of anxieties, tracking the invisible war being waged within our own immune systems. This compulsive enumeration becomes a kind of ritual, a way of measuring mortality in increments small enough to be bearable. If we cannot comprehend death as a single, overwhelming fact, perhaps we can manage it as a series of countable losses—strand by strand, break by break, cell by cell.

What emerges from these juxtapositions—the marquee's flippant question, the anxious buzzer, the compulsive counting—is a portrait of ordinary people going about their unconscious daily routines while carrying, often unknowingly, the weight of profound existential questions. The woman checking her hairline in the mirror, the man wincing at an old fracture, the patient awaiting lab results: these are not separate from the deepest human concerns about meaning, mortality, and judgment. Rather, they are the very sites where such concerns take up residence. The text suggests, ultimately, that we need not seek out grand philosophical settings to encounter life's largest questions. They are already here, embedded in our marquees and radio dials, our morning mirrors and medical charts—waiting, quietly, to be noticed.
outputs.L4:
# Where Are We Going?

The commuters shuffle past each morning, faces blank behind newspapers and phone screens, moving toward destinations that seem, on closer inspection, entirely arbitrary. Office towers rise like question marks against the grey sky. A roadside sign flickers: TURN LEFT FOR MEANING, or perhaps it says something else entirely—the letters blur in the rearview mirror, half-formed, unreadable.

Someone has spray-painted JESUS SAVES across the underpass, the letters dripping red like an afterthought or a warning. Further down, another sign, smaller, hand-lettered: ARE YOU READY? Ready for what, exactly? The question hangs in the exhaust fumes, unanswered, perhaps unanswerable. A church marquee advertises ETERNAL LIFE — INQUIRE WITHIN, as if salvation were a transaction to be conducted at a folding table, cash or credit accepted.

The ambiguity multiplies. Every arrow points somewhere and nowhere. Every gospel tract left on a bus seat promises a destination that no one can verify, a place at the end of all places. And yet the commuters keep moving, keep arriving, keep departing, as though the not-knowing were simply another Tuesday.

---

And so, in the absence of any answer to *where*, the counting begins.

Fourteen grey hairs this month, up from eleven the month before. Four hundred and twelve T-cells, according to the last blood draw, a number that means everything and nothing, that the doctor recites like a psalm. Three new scars—one from the kitchen knife, one from the bicycle, one whose origin has been forgotten entirely, erased by time the way water erases footprints on sand.

Two thousand three hundred and ninety-one days since the funeral. Six hundred and forty-seven days since the diagnosis. Nineteen days since the last cigarette, a number that resets sometimes, slides backward, begins again from zero with grim, quiet persistence.

The body keeps its own ledger. Wounds heal and are tallied. Cells divide and are tallied. Mornings accumulate, pill bottles empty, birthdays arrive with their small, cruel arithmetic—another year, another wrinkle, another gray hair to add to the fourteen, soon to be fifteen, sixteen, an ascending column with no visible sum.

This is the human answer to the unanswerable question of destination: to count what can be counted. To measure the graying, the healing, the days survived, as though enough decimal points might approximate a purpose. As though four hundred and twelve T-cells might, multiplied by some hidden factor, yield the coordinates of *where we are going*.

But the counting does not resolve the ambiguity—it only dresses it in numbers. The commuters still move without certainty. The signs still point in contradictory directions. JESUS SAVES and ARE YOU READY and TURN LEFT FOR MEANING remain suspended, unresolved, while beneath them, in the small print of the body, someone tallies grey hairs, T-cells, wounds, and days, building a fragile architecture of order against the vast, indifferent uncertainty of it all.
outputs.L5:
# Dear Conflicted Reader

I understand you're writing to me because something inside you feels pulled in two directions at once. Perhaps it's a decision you cannot make, a truth you're afraid to admit, or a version of yourself you don't recognize in the mirror some mornings.

Conflict, despite its uncomfortable nature, often signals that we care about more than one thing. If you felt nothing, there would be no tension—no tug-of-war between what you want and what you think you should want, between the safe path and the one that terrifies you into feeling alive.

I won't pretend to have a tidy answer for you, because conflicted feelings rarely resolve into neat conclusions. Instead, I'd ask you to sit with the discomfort a little longer before rushing toward resolution. What is each side of your conflict trying to protect? Sometimes one voice speaks for security, another for authenticity. Sometimes one honors the past, another reaches toward who you're becoming.

There's no shame in being torn. It means you're paying attention to the complexity of your own life rather than accepting easy, prepackaged answers. The people who never feel conflicted are often the ones who've stopped listening to parts of themselves.

So, dear reader, don't rush to silence the conflict. Let it speak. Write down what each side is saying, without judgment. Ask which voice has been quieter, more neglected, more afraid to be heard. That may be the one worth listening to first.

Whatever you decide, know this: uncertainty is not weakness. It's proof that you're wrestling with something real.

With warmth and patience,
A Fellow Traveler in Doubt

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem addressed to "My Dear Conflicted Reader" that mixes observations of small-town Southern life with a meditation on fate and free will, ending in a repetitive "count your..." litany.
counterfactuals.output:
**My Dear Conflicted Reader,**

I write to you from the porch of a house that has settled into its foundation the way an old dog settles into afternoon shade—not out of choice, exactly, but because the bones have learned where they belong. Down the road, the Baptist church and the Methodist church stare at each other like siblings who stopped speaking over an inheritance, and between them the gas station sells boiled peanuts and scratch-off tickets to men who believe equally in Jesus and luck, not seeing the contradiction, or seeing it and loving it anyway.

You want to know if we choose our lives or if they choose us. I watch Miss Ruthie water plastic flowers on a grave every Sunday, rain or shine, and I think: maybe both. Maybe she chose grief the way the kudzu chose that dead oak—slowly, inevitably, until you can't tell which one is holding the other up. The teenagers still drag Main Street on Friday nights in trucks their daddies drove before them, tracing the same six blocks like a liturgy, and who's to say if they're rebelling or fulfilling prophecy, if the boy who leaves for the Army and the boy who stays and takes over the hardware store were ever really choosing at all, or just becoming what the town had already written for them in its ledger of names and needs.

I don't know if God deals the cards or if we're just good at pretending the hand we're dealt was the one we wanted. I've seen too many men swear they built themselves from nothing while standing on land their grandfather cleared with someone else's labor. I've seen too many women call it destiny when it was just the only door left unlocked.

But here's what I know, dear reader, torn as you are between the comfort of fate and the terror of freedom, between the notion that it was all meant to be and the darker thought that it was all just us, fumbling, choosing wrong turns dressed up as right ones: the tomatoes still ripen in July whether we deserve them or not. The cicadas still split their skins on the same trees each June like clockwork, like doom, like grace.

So count your blessings, and count your losses.
Count the church bells and count the empty pews.
Count the fireflies you caught as a child and let go, and the ones you didn't.
Count the years since you left this town, or the years since you stayed.
Count your father's hands, your mother's silences, the miles between who you were told to be and who you became.
Count your regrets like rosary beads, worn smooth from handling.
Count your mercies, small and stubborn as weeds through concrete.
Count the stars, if you can still see them past the streetlight—
and count, too, my dear reader, the moments you'll never know
whether you chose, or whether they chose you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of literary fiction that opens with a direct address to the reader about human indecision, includes a church marquee joke about heaven and smoking, and closes with an escalating list of things to "count."
counterfactuals.output:
**What We Almost Do**

You know this about yourself, don't you—that you are a creature of almost. You have stood in doorways longer than necessary, one foot in and one foot out, weighing a room before committing to it. You have held the phone to your ear, thumb hovering over the red circle, rehearsing goodbyes you never quite deliver. Indecision is not a failure of courage, though it wears that costume well. It is closer to a kind of prayer—the belief that if you wait long enough, the universe will make the choice for you, and you will be absolved of having chosen at all.

Ruth Anne Dill was a woman of almost.

She had almost left Wexford twice—once at twenty-two with a boy named Casey who drove a truck the color of a bruise, and once at thirty-four with nothing but a duffel bag and a tank of gas, turning around at the county line because the sun was setting and she didn't want to arrive anywhere in the dark. Now she was forty-one, and she stood most mornings at the window of the Wexford Diner, coffee going cold in her hand, watching the marquee across the street change its letters like a mouth trying out new shapes.

The church was First Baptist, small and white-sided, its sign presided over by Pastor Timmons, a man who believed humor was next to godliness. That week the marquee read:

**SMOKING IN HEAVEN? WE'D HAVE TO ASK ABOUT THAT UPSTAIRS.**

Ruth Anne laughed the first time she saw it, a short huff through her nose, coffee steam fogging the glass. Her father had died of lungs gone black as a chimney flue, still lighting one off the end of another in the driveway two weeks before the end, defiant as a man could be about a thing that was killing him. She thought about telling Pastor Timmons that joke wasn't as clean as he thought it was. She thought about a lot of things she didn't do.

The diner door chime rang. It was Wallace Pruitt, seventy-six years old, who had asked her to marry him eleven days ago in this same booth, over the same cold coffee, and who she had not yet answered.

"Morning, Ruthie."

"Wallace."

He didn't ask again. That was the terrible kindness of him—he had decided to let her almost forever if that's what she needed, and something about that decision, so plainly made and so plainly *his*, needling at her like a hook she couldn't work free.

She thought: I could say yes right now. I could say it before the coffee's poured.

She didn't.

Outside, the marquee letters clacked as the Pastor's boy climbed the ladder to swap them out for Sunday's sermon title. Ruth Anne watched him work, watched the black plastic letters go up one by one, and she thought about all the things a person could count instead of deciding anything at all.

She could count the letters on the marquee—eleven, twelve, thirteen.

She could count the rings in Wallace's coffee cup, the pale brown circles stacked like tree years.

She could count the mornings she had stood at this window, which by her rough math came to something over four thousand.

She could count the words she had almost said to him, stacking up somewhere behind her teeth like unmailed letters, and the years behind those words, and the length of her father's driveway where he stood smoking in the cold not caring what it cost him, and the space between *yes* and *not yet*, which was either the shortest distance in the world or the longest, and the exact number of days a woman could stand in a doorway before the doorway simply became her home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental short prose text combining epistolary tone, wry religious satire (like a church sign pun), and a rhythmic catalog of bodily and everyday counting rituals.
counterfactuals.output:
# Letter to the Congregation Regarding Numbers, Sunday, Late

Dear ones who count,

The sign out front still says WORTH IS WORTH WAITING FOR, though the R fell off in March and no one's climbed the ladder since. I confess: I have been counting things instead of praying, which the pamphlet says is the same act performed with less faith and more fingers.

I count my heartbeat against the hymn tempo and find I am always one behind, a half-step in arrears to God, like rent.

I count the ceiling tiles during the sermon — one hundred and forty-four, a nice biblical number, twelve twelves, the fence of the New Jerusalem laid flat and stapled above Pastor Lyle's head while he explains grace using a football metaphor.

I count on my hands the days since I last meant anything I said out loud in this building. I run out of hands.

Body, keep the census: ten fingers, ten toes, one tongue that lies in increments, thirty-two teeth (I am told; I have never verified), two eyes closing at the same rate as the collection plate goes around — everyone counting bills under the pew light like it's a confession booth with better lighting.

The sign should say: ALL ARE WELCOME (TERMS APPLY).

I keep my own ledger. Sundays attended: eleven of the last fifty-two. Casseroles brought to the Whitfield funeral: one, and it had the wrong number of eggs, I could taste the deficit. Times I have said *Lord* and meant *laundry*: uncountable, they rhyme in the mouth if you're tired enough.

Here is my counting rosary, the one they didn't teach us:
one for the alarm clock,
two for the coffee,
three for the four texts I won't answer,
five for the mirror where I check my own face like a scale reading,
six seven eight for the stairs down to where the car won't start,
nine for the Our Father recited at a red light,
ten for the sin of arriving anyway.

The bulletin this week has a typo: it says God's mercy is *infinite*, but the font is size 10, condensed, like even the mercy had to be shrunk to fit the margins allotted by the printer's budget.

I want to tell you the tally comes out even. It doesn't. I want to tell you grace is the number after the last number, but I have only ever counted up to where I stopped believing and called that a total.

The sign should say nothing. Some things shouldn't rhyme with themselves in public.

Still, I'll be there next Sunday, is what I'm saying. Eleven becomes twelve. Twelve is a fence too. I'll bring the right number of eggs this time. I am trying, in my fashion, to close the ledger evenly, though I suspect the ledger was never a ledger — just a rosary I didn't recognize, counted on hands I keep mistaking for my own.

Faithfully (in the actuarial sense),
A Parishioner Who Keeps Score
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a stream-of-consciousness narrative voice that begins "My Dear Conflicted Reader," references a road scene with contrasting characters, quotes an ironic church marquee, and ends with a chant-like list of things to count, from grey hairs to T cells.
counterfactuals.output:
My Dear Conflicted Reader,

so here we go again, headlights and gravel and that particular hour when the sky can't decide if it's still holding onto blue or letting the whole thing go to black, and I'm driving, or someone's driving, past the intersection where the man in the wheelchair sells roses out of a bucket and the woman in the Lexus doesn't roll her window down but her son does, small hand, small flower, small transaction that means everything and nothing, and across the street the marquee outside First Baptist says GOD ANSWERS KNEE-MAIL in letters some volunteer arranged with what I imagine were trembling, well-intentioned hands, and I want to laugh but the laugh gets caught on something, catches like fabric on a nail, because isn't that the whole joke, the whole terrible joke, that we're all just sending up prayers like text messages, like anyone's checking their phone up there, like the signal even reaches—

and the rose-seller's cardboard sign says GOD BLESS in letters not nearly so clever, no pun, just need, just plain need sitting there in Sharpie, and I think about need versus cleverness, about how the marquee people get to be clever because their need is handled, is housed, is fed, and I keep driving because that's what you do, you keep driving, you keep the car between the lines even when your mind is doing something else entirely, is doing this—

is counting.

count the grey hairs, seventeen this month I think, maybe twenty, sprouting up like they're staging a coup, a slow rebellion of pigment giving up the ghost
count the birthdays left if the actuarial tables are honest, if the doctor's face when he read the numbers meant what I think it meant
count the miles between here and the place I used to call home before home became a verb I couldn't conjugate anymore
count the excuses I gave for not calling her back, stack them like the coins I don't have
count the T cells, count them like sheep, like soldiers, like the only army I've got left, rising, falling, rising, please rising—

count, count, count,
my dear conflicted reader,
because counting is a kind of praying too,
and maybe that's the only mail
God ever really answers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Southern Gothic-style vignette in second person that blends humor and dread, referencing predestination, a radio ministry, and a cumulative list poem of things one might count in daily life.
counterfactuals.output:
You wake before the fan stops working, which is the only mercy God extends to you on a Tuesday. The window unit rattles like something trying to get out of a coffin, and Brother Wendell Teague is already on the radio, has been on the radio since 5 AM, has perhaps never not been on the radio, explaining in his gravel-and-honey voice that you were chosen before the foundation of the world, chosen the way a man chooses which chicken gets the hatchet, and there is nothing you can do about it now, bless your heart, so you might as well have some coffee.

You do not find this comforting. You have never found this comforting. Your grandmother found it comforting the way she found copperheads comforting — something to be respected, given wide berth, occasionally used to explain why Uncle Dale drowned in four inches of creek water. "It was written," she'd say, snapping beans on the porch, and you were never sure if she meant in scripture or in the county paper.

So you count things. This is what you do instead of thinking about election and reprobation and the terrible math of grace. You count because counting is the one form of prayer that doesn't require you to know, ahead of time, whether you're the wheat or the chaff.

You count the cicada husks on the porch rail, seven, then eight, translucent and split down the back like something escaped its own indictment.

You count the cicada husks and the flies at the screen door, patient as debt collectors.

You count the cicada husks, the flies at the screen door, and the number of times Brother Teague says the word "vessel" before you finish your eggs — three, and it's not even 6:30.

You count the cicada husks, the flies, the vessels, and the church bulletins stacked on the dash of your daddy's truck, soft with damp, going back to a revival in 1987 that nobody survived unchanged.

You count the cicada husks, the flies, the vessels, the bulletins, and the jars of tomatoes your mother put up the summer she started forgetting things, each one dated in her handwriting, getting worse, like she was leaving you a record of her own erosion.

You count the cicada husks, the flies, the vessels, the bulletins, the jars, and the Sundays since anybody in this family took communion without flinching.

You count the cicada husks, the flies, the vessels, the bulletins, the jars, the Sundays, and the names on the family stone out past the tobacco barn, where the kudzu is winning, where it has always been winning, patient as predestination itself, and you understand that the vine doesn't care whether the tree was elect or reprobate. It grows over both the same.

Brother Teague says the offering plate is a vessel too, that everything is a vessel, that you yourself are being filled or emptied at this very moment and the difference was decided before your mother was decided, before the creek that took Uncle Dale had a name.

You turn off the radio. The silence has kudzu in it too.

You keep counting anyway — the flies, the jars, the names — because a man's got to do something with his hands while he waits to find out what he was for.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
